title: Sisney v. State
summary: An inmate was not entitled to enforce the state’s general food-service contract because the court found no clear contractual intent to grant him an individual enforcement right.
notes: The editors expressly question how recipients of promised kosher food can be classified as incidental and ask about the consequences of allowing suit against different defendants. The court’s characterization is therefore presented as its contested reasoning, not as a self-evident description of the contract’s purpose.

sections.Parties: Charles Sisney was a Jewish inmate seeking contract damages. The defendants were South Dakota, prison official Douglas Weber, and CBM, the private food-service provider contracting with the state.
sections.Material Facts:
The state contracted with CBM to provide food services at correctional facilities. The agreement described service to the state, addressed residents’ and staff needs, set a caloric standard, and required substitutions accommodating religious dietary restrictions. After a change in kosher meals, Sisney alleged that the meals supplied several hundred fewer calories than required and failed to meet his religious requirements. His administrative grievances were rejected.

Sisney relied on the contract’s direct effect on him and on its reference to a complaint-resolution process. That process, however, was the institution’s general grievance procedure, available independently of this contract. The agreement did not expressly state that individual inmates could enforce it.
sections.Procedural History: The circuit court dismissed for failure to state a claim, accepting the pleaded facts but concluding that Sisney lacked third-party-beneficiary status. The South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed in 2008. The opinion resolves this contract-enforcement claim rather than determining whether the alleged diet complied with constitutional or other independent duties.
sections.Issue: Did the contract’s food and religious-accommodation requirements make Sisney an intended beneficiary with a private right to sue for breach?
sections.Holding: No. Under the court’s interpretation of the state beneficiary statute and public-contract principles, the agreement did not clearly grant the asserted individual benefit and enforcement status.
sections.Reasoning:
A benefit from performance and a right to enforce the promise are separate matters. Public contracts commonly benefit many people, and the court applied a presumption against exposing a private government contractor to actions by every person benefiting from its work. It required a clear expression of the relevant intent.

The food-service agreement was characterized as serving the state’s institutional needs, with inmates receiving incidental benefits for purposes of contract enforcement. Its grievance provision did not change that result because it referred to an independent general administrative process. The court accordingly found the pleaded contractual language insufficient even while assuming Sisney’s factual account for dismissal purposes.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: The comparison with Sisney v. Reisch is essential. The same inmate and similar food problem produced a different result under a different agreement.

topics.third-party-beneficiaries: Distinguishes practical benefits under a public contract from an individual right to enforce it.
topics.interpretation: Makes the contract’s expressed purpose and enforcement language decisive.
topics.public-contracts: Applies the court’s restrictive presumption for members of the public.
